opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think MiMo is one of the more interesting stories in the open model ecosystem right now, partly because Xiaomi wasn't a name most people in the West associated with frontier language model work. It shows how deep the Chinese bench has become. It's not just DeepSeek, Qwen, Moonshot, and Zhipu anymore. A consumer electronics company can stand up a team and, within a fairly short window, ship models that are genuinely competitive, especially on reasoning and math-heavy benchmarks at smaller parameter counts.

A few things stand out to me. First, the playbook has diffused. Post-training recipes, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, careful data curation for reasoning, all of that used to feel like secret sauce at a handful of labs. Now it's well enough understood, partly thanks to open papers and open weights, that a well-resourced team with good people can execute on it quickly. MiMo is evidence of that.

Second, Xiaomi has a real strategic reason to do this. They have phones, cars, smart home devices, a huge hardware footprint. Owning your own models, especially efficient ones that could eventually run on-device or close to it, makes sense for them. So this isn't a vanity project; there's a product logic underneath it.

Third, and this is what I care about most, they're releasing openly, and that matters for the ecosystem. Every strong open-weight release from China raises the bar for what Western open models need to look like. I've been pretty vocal that the US risks falling behind in open models, not because we lack talent, but because the incentives at the big American labs push toward closed releases. When companies like Xiaomi enter and contribute, researchers everywhere default to building on those models, and that has long-term consequences for who shapes the research agenda.

The caveat I'd add is that benchmark scores at release don't always tell the full story. The real test is whether people actually adopt these models, fine-tune them, and find them robust in practice. Some models look great on paper and then fade. So I'd watch the downstream usage, the derivative models on Hugging Face, the developer mindshare. But as a signal, MiMo tells you the frontier of capable open models is getting more crowded, and the competition is increasingly coming from places people didn't expect.

r001.rationale: The response says MiMo came from an unexpected entrant and that open-model competition is getting more crowded, but it does not clearly suggest that observers have yet to internalize that new models will keep appearing.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think MiMo is one of the more interesting stories in open models this year, and I don't think it's gotten the attention it deserves in the West. When Xiaomi first showed up with the MiMo-7B reasoning models, a lot of people shrugged, because it's easy to dismiss a phone and appliance company as a tourist in this space. But the pace since then has been striking. They went from a small team doing a credible reasoning model to shipping larger, more complete releases with pretraining details, RL recipes, and actual weights, and that's the part I care about.

The thing I keep coming back to is that MiMo fits a pattern we've seen with Chinese labs more broadly. DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM, and now Xiaomi are all converging on a similar playbook: heavy investment in pretraining data quality, reasoning-focused RL, and then releasing openly because open weights are how you build mindshare when you don't have a frontier consumer product people already live in. Xiaomi is a little different because they do have distribution. They have hundreds of millions of phones and a whole ecosystem of devices, so the model doesn't have to win on benchmarks alone to be strategically useful. A good on-device or near-device model that's tuned for their hardware is a real asset even if it never tops a leaderboard.

What I'd caution against is reading too much into any single release. The gap between a strong open model and the frontier labs is still real, especially on the long-horizon agentic stuff. But the gap between the Chinese open ecosystem and American open models has basically inverted over the last two years. If you'd told me in 2023 that the best open weights I could download would mostly come from China, and that a company known for rice cookers would be a legitimate contributor, I would have been skeptical. Now it just seems like the natural result of a lot of capable people, cheap compute relative to their ambitions, and a policy environment that treats open release as a national advantage rather than a liability.

So the way I view MiMo is less as a surprise and more as a signal. It tells you how deep the bench is. If Xiaomi can do this, the number of organizations that can train a serious model is much larger than people in the Valley tend to assume, and that should change how we think about where the open ecosystem goes from here.

r001.rationale: The response says Xiaomi’s release reveals a larger-than-assumed pool of organizations able to train serious models, but it does not clearly state that observers have yet to internalize that more models like MiMo will continue to appear.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a sign of how quickly the competitive landscape can change. Xiaomi isn’t a company people have traditionally put at the center of the language-model conversation, so seeing MiMo emerge makes you reconsider where strong teams and models might come from.

But I’d separate the excitement around a release from the question of how durable that progress is. How well does the model work when people actually use it? Can the team follow it up with another strong release? What does it cost to serve? Those are the things I’d watch before drawing a big conclusion.

Xiaomi also has an interesting potential advantage in distribution. If you can put useful models into products people already use, you have a path from research to actual adoption. That makes them worth watching, beyond whatever position a particular model holds on a leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The response says MiMo’s emergence makes people reconsider where strong models may come from, but it does not suggest observers have yet to internalize that new models like it will keep appearing.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the pace of releases from what we can actually conclude about the models. You can see a new model family emerge very quickly, but understanding how capable it is takes longer. I’d want to look at the training details, what they release, and how the models perform when people actually use them.

For me, the interesting question with Xiaomi is whether this becomes a sustained effort. A strong first release gets attention. Consistently improving the models, making them useful to developers, and integrating them into products—that’s what would make it significant. I wouldn’t draw a big conclusion from the speed of emergence alone.

r001.rationale: The response notes Xiaomi’s rapid emergence and asks whether its effort will be sustained, but does not say observers have yet to internalize that new models will keep appearing.
